## Chapter 16: Basic Six Sigma Team Management

### Building a Six Sigma Team

You can't just have a team ready ahead of time to start working on every project that comes up. Six Sigma teams need to be uniquely tailored to the goals and processes at hand. The same Six Sigma specialists — Black Belt leaders, data analysts, or project managers — might work on multiple projects, but individual subject-matter experts and team members only bring high value to the team if they're familiar with the process or have some education, knowledge, or skill to offer that's related to it. Not every team member will serve consistently throughout a project's whole life, either. That's often why companies send existing employees to Six Sigma training instead of hiring Six Sigma specialists.

Executive leadership groups working with Six Sigma leaders and specialists generally assemble the teams. Any process improvement team should have, at minimum:

- A Six Sigma leader
- A process owner
- A process specialist
- Someone to manage budget and accounting

Some of these roles might be filled by the same person; the process owner might also be the process specialist. Depending on expected needs, the team might also need to include technical resources, like a programmer or IT lead, as well as individuals from human resources, compliance, legal, or other supporting departments.

#### Three Types of Team Members

When assembling teams, organizations should remember there are three basic types of team member with respect to a Six Sigma project. First, there are regular team members. These individuals take part in every team activity and attend all or nearly all team meetings. Regular team members include project leaders, process owners and specialists, and identified subject-matter experts the team or executives consider critical components of their group.

Second, ad hoc team members provide expertise as needed. These are generally subject-matter experts or employees who work directly with the process. You don't want to pull these employees away from their job duties for every team event, since that would negatively impact current production. Instead, these employees are brought into team meetings as needed, when additional information or assistance is required.

Finally, resource team members are only brought in when the project team leader feels they're needed at a meeting or team event to provide specialized information, advice, or help accessing resources. Resource team members are generally members of supporting departments, like accounting, human resources, or compliance. Resource team members might also be managers or leaders in departments related to the process being improved. For example, if a team is looking to improve a customer service department, it might need help with inputs from the marketing department; someone from marketing could be added as a resource team member.

#### Tips for Selecting Team Members

Most Six Sigma process improvement teams are relatively small: five regular members is considered a good average number. Adding too many regular members can create communication problems, make brainstorming sessions harder to manage, and cause burnout. When every Six Sigma team at a company is large, there's a good chance team members are serving on multiple projects. While ad hoc or resource members can serve several projects and handle their own daily work, regular team members shouldn't be asked to serve on more than one team while also handling daily workloads. In fact, organizational leaders might want to consider reducing work requirements for team members serving as full-time members on a project.

Other tips for selecting team members include:

- Choose employees who have knowledge of the customer, product, or process related to the project.
- Choose employees who've shown willingness and ability to work toward improvement in a team setting.
- Select employees who have access to, and understanding of, the data needed to learn about and measure the process or problem.
- Choose employees who can provide at least five hours of work a week to the team.
- Match employee skills to the projects at hand; if a project will likely involve only technical improvements, you'd have less reason to add a team member skilled in marketing.
- Remove political obstacles through team selection; if a specific person at an organization is likely to be an obstacle for a team, sometimes putting that person on the team can increase the chance they'll buy into the process.

### Team Member Roles

The team member roles described in this section are based on Six Sigma process improvement best practices, but best practices also say teams and team leaders shouldn't be overly rigid. Experienced Six Sigma leaders and specialists understand how to work within best practices while also building unique team structures tailored to the project or process at hand.

**Sponsors and Champions**

We've already briefly touched on sponsors and champions in earlier chapters. In most Six Sigma settings, these are the senior-level leaders overseeing projects at the highest level. Even the Black Belt needs to report to the project's sponsor or champion. The senior leader is generally responsible for a project's final outcome, which means they generally want regular progress reports; sometimes the sponsor or champion is the link between the team and the leadership board. As a senior leader, the champion or sponsor is also responsible for helping the team get funding and resources to ensure the project's success. A few additional responsibilities in this role include:

- Guiding the team, particularly during the project charter phase. The sponsor often provides input on what's in a project's scope and who can be included on a team.
- Locating resources for the team, including support from other departments, money, equipment, time, and work hours.
- Handling political issues within a corporate structure, so the team doesn't have to.
- Working with other managers within the organization to help the team succeed at improving a process and transitioning the improvements into a day-to-day work setting.

**Business or Process Owners**

The business or process owner is generally someone directly responsible for the process in a leadership role. Generally, the process owner is the person who'll "receive" a solution implemented by a Six Sigma team, once that solution is ready to be rolled out to every team member or used daily. Because of that, the process owner is generally included on the team, since they need to understand how and why any change is made. The process owner also needs to be familiar with the control methods created by the Six Sigma team, since they'll become responsible for maintaining and monitoring those controls once the process moves from a team setting into daily production.

A process owner also generally acts as the process specialist on a Six Sigma team. The process owner has insight into the existing process, understands the needs of customers and employees tied to the process, and might already have access to data about the process. The process owner isn't always the only process specialist on a team, though; in some cases, the person who owns the process doesn't have enough day-to-day interaction with the process to be a specialist.

When leading or managing a Six Sigma team, Black Belts and others need to watch out for process owners resistant to change or who believe they have all the answers. Someone used to their own ways might not want to involve other team members, or might believe certain changes are "impossible" just because they're new. Some leaders who are also process owners might fear a team member outshining them or threatening their position, which can lead them to block team member participation. These are a few of the political and human resources problems Six Sigma leaders face, and Black Belts and project leaders need to work tactfully with champions, sponsors, and process managers to resolve these issues.

**Six Sigma Leaders**

Six Sigma projects are generally led by certified Black Belts, though some organizations let Green Belts act as leaders on smaller initiatives, with occasional feedback and guidance from Black Belts. At most organizations, the Black Belt holds primary responsibility for the regular work carried out by a team and generally works with only one team or project at a time.

The best scenarios let organizations align Black Belts with projects in areas they're already familiar with. For example, a bank might have several Black Belts on staff. Each Black Belt might specialize in working with certain processes or departments; one might generally work with compliance and audit processes, another with accounting, a third with customer-facing processes, and a fourth with online processes. Since Black Belt resources can be limited, this isn't always possible. Most certified Black Belts can bring Six Sigma methods to process improvements even in areas they aren't closely familiar with. In some cases, several managers or other individuals are certified as Black Belts and might lead processes beyond their regular responsibilities, though this can place an undue burden on employees and isn't always the best solution.

Black Belt project leaders often work to:

- Help build a justification for a project.
- Provide input on selecting project team members.
- Lead teams through every DMAIC phase, covered in depth in PART IV.
- Educate and support team members as they learn about and use Six Sigma tools.
- Provide oversight through time management, decision-making, and planning.
- Maintain timelines and deadlines, sometimes together with a certified Project Manager.
- Provide expertise in the form of statistical analysis or guidance with analysis.
- Assist with the project's transition.
- Report to the sponsor or champion regularly.
- Provide documentation at the project's end.

At some organizations, Master Black Belts play a general role leading multiple Six Sigma projects. Master Black Belts act as coaches for multiple teams; Black Belts leading Six Sigma teams might work with Master Black Belts to solve especially difficult problems or seek help with complex statistical analyses. Master Black Belts provide ongoing education for both Black Belts and Green Belts, helping team members constantly improve their understanding of Six Sigma methodologies.

**Project Managers**

Some organizations use traditional project management techniques alongside Six Sigma improvement methodologies. At these organizations, a project manager is generally assigned to a Six Sigma project. Although structures vary by organization, the project manager generally doesn't lead the team. Instead, the PM (Project Manager) offers leadership support to the Black Belt, keeping documentation and timelines up to date, helping keep meetings on track, and making sure items are followed up on after meetings. At first glance, you might think adding a PM to a team would cause problems for a Black Belt, but when the two roles work together, the Black Belt benefits. With a PM worrying about timelines or whether the meeting is drifting too far off track, a Six Sigma specialist is free to focus on the brainstorming session or statistical analysis at hand.

**Timekeeper**

Not every Six Sigma team uses timekeepers, but they can help keep meetings on track, reduce the chance of scope creep, and increase overall productivity. The timekeeper can be anyone on the team not regularly engaged in leading meetings, brainstorming activities, or logging team activities and notes. The timekeeper shouldn't police time so rigidly that the benefits of fluid discussion and brainstorming are lost, but should gently steer teams toward following the agenda's timing or give the project leader an indication that time for the topic at hand has run out.

To work properly, a timekeeper needs an agenda to follow. It's generally the Black Belt's or project manager's responsibility to provide a detailed agenda for each meeting. The agenda should include clear indications of how long each item should take, though teams should always be aware that agendas can change during the meeting, at the project manager's or leader's discretion.

Team leaders should choose an organized, level-headed timekeeper. In the heat of discussions and debates, it's easy for any team member to lose track of time — and the timekeeper is a team member too. Beyond their regular duties as a team member, the timekeeper is expected to:

- Keep an eye on the agenda and the time
- Warn team members when time for a given agenda item is nearly up; teams might want to set a five-minute warning rule, to give themselves a few minutes to wrap up a discussion
- Signal that time is up for a given discussion or item

Although project leaders might choose to ignore the agenda, they should also support the timekeeper's ability to politely interrupt. Timekeepers can't do their job if they're scolded by other team members for noting the time.

**Scribes or Note-Takers**

A lot of discussion happens in the middle of brainstorming sessions and Six Sigma team meetings, and someone needs to log that information. Notes matter because they help team members review what was discussed, build follow-up lists and action items from a discussion, and record charts, tables, and diagrams created during brainstorming processes. Although anyone can take notes, the team leader should name one person as the team's official scribe. Sometimes this person is a certified project manager working alongside a Six Sigma team leader. Other times, it's a team member seen as detail-oriented and organized.

The Black Belt or other project leader should never be the scribe; it's too hard to take notes while leading a discussion or exercise. The Black Belt might take a few notes during the discussion, but will likely miss important details while working directly with other team members.

The scribe should create typed meeting notes or minutes and distribute those notes to every team member as soon as possible after a meeting. Team members can review the notes and add any missing information, if they want; organizations often build portals or shared file systems so teams can keep notes and every other document in one easily accessible place.

One challenge in logging a Six Sigma project meeting's discussions is recording the diagrams and brainstorming that happened. This is especially true if teams use whiteboards, paper, or sticky notes to build diagrams; the scribe doesn't always have the skills or software to recreate a computerized version of such documents. One tip for logging this information, used by many modern Six Sigma teams, is taking a photo of the diagrams with a smartphone or digital camera. The images can then be uploaded to the team's shared workspace; if needed, a Black Belt or Green Belt can convert the raw diagrams into a computerized version for the purpose of presenting information to leadership or other departments, if desired.

**Team Members**

Earlier in this chapter, we covered the three main types of team member: regular, ad hoc, and resource. Selecting members for each of these roles falls to the project leader, the sponsor or champion, and the overall organizational leadership team. Beyond the project leader, process owner, and process specialist, Six Sigma teams generally consist of one to three other regular members. Beyond serving as timekeeper or scribe as directed by the team leader, team members also:

- Take part in brainstorming sessions, discussions, and other team activities.
- Collect data and run analyses under the Black Belt's direction. Team members carrying out these duties are often Green Belts.
- Do work between meetings, as required by the project leader.
- Report the results and progress of individual tasks to the team.
- Review work carried out by other team members and the team as a whole, offering suggestions and feedback.

### Timelines, Scheduling, and Milestones

Scheduling and keeping to that timeline is an integral part of the Six Sigma project process. Organizational leaders need to understand how long a project will take, when results can be expected, and when team resources will free up for other undertakings. Without this information, leadership can't plan continuous improvement, and employees can feel trapped in a project that seems to drag on forever. In this section, we'll cover two methods for building a project timeline or schedule and touch on the importance of milestones.

#### Phase-Based Timeline

Six Sigma projects generally follow a specific series of phases; we've already briefly introduced the DMAIC method's concept. DMAIC splits a project into five phases: Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, and Control. Experienced Six Sigma specialists, with some data and information about a project and process, can generally provide a pretty basic, rough time estimate, assigning a certain number of weeks to each phase. It's also worth noting that most phases will likely overlap.

To build a rough project timeline, a Black Belt or other Six Sigma leader generally starts with an overall time requirement. They estimate the total time needed for an improvement, or work with a deadline imposed by the leadership group. For example, the leadership group might say an improvement needs to be finished within four months.

Using a four-month timeline and the information already available about the process, problem, and resources, the Black Belt can build an estimated DMAIC-process timeline that looks like the figure below.

<img alt="16-week DMAIC phase schedule: Define (weeks 1-3), Measure (weeks 3-8), Analyze (weeks 6-10), Improve (weeks 9-14), Control (weeks 13-16)" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:563px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


The estimated timeline is 16 weeks; the specialist believes the Define phase will take 3 weeks and the Measure phase will take 5. The Measure phase overlaps with both the Define and Analyze phases, which is normal in Six Sigma projects.

The benefit of this approach is that you can generate a timeline quickly. The downsides are that someone without Six Sigma experience and a good understanding of the process being improved can easily misjudge the time needed for each phase, and leadership might treat this as a fixed timeline, which can create unrealistic expectations. When presenting such a timeline, make sure everyone knows it's a rough estimate and that the time for each phase can change throughout the process.

#### Critical Path Method

The critical path method is a more detailed way of setting timelines for various elements of a project, but it requires more information and input from a project team. That means you likely won't be able to provide a detailed timeline until the project is underway; a critical path diagram might be one of the activities the team carries out as part of the Define phase.

**Building a Critical Path Diagram**

A critical path diagram can be built for a whole project or for each phase of a project. As we walk through the steps of building a critical path diagram, we'll use as an example the Define phase of a project to reduce bad debt (uncollected invoices) in a medical billing setting.

1. **Identify the critical needs or activities to complete the project or project phase.** To complete the define phase of our bad-debt improvement project in a medical billing setting, the team needs to choose a team, charter the project, define the problem, and create a baseline metric.
2. **Put the critical activities in order.** The order in which the team should carry out the tasks defined in step one is: Choose a team; charter the project and define the problem (these tasks can be done simultaneously); create a baseline metric.
3. **Assign a time to each task.** A Six Sigma specialist estimates it'll take one week to choose a team, one week to build a charter, one day to build a problem statement, and two weeks to build a baseline metric.
4. **Diagram the tasks, stacking simultaneous or parallel processes and including the time figures.** The diagram is built left to right. Items on the left need to be completed before items on the right can be completed. When items can be done at the same time, they're stacked.

<img alt="Define-phase tasks with no connections: Choose Team (1 week), Create problem statement (1 day), Charter the project (1 week), Create baseline metric (2 weeks)" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


1. **Trace a critical path through the diagram.** When steps are stacked, the critical path runs through the step with the longest time estimate. For example, the team can build a problem statement while working on the project charter; the project charter takes Monday through Friday to complete. The problem statement is ready on Tuesday. However, the team doesn't finish every step in that series until the project charter is done.

<img alt="Define-phase tasks connected by the critical path: Choose Team → Charter the project → Create baseline metric, with Create problem statement in parallel" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


1. **Add up the longest times from each section.** In this case, the team adds up 1 week, 1 week, and 2 weeks to get a total of 4 weeks for the Define phase.

We used a fairly simple example, but you can use the critical path method to estimate timelines for extremely complex projects or processes.

#### Milestone Meetings

Once a timeline is set, set up milestone meetings and dates to help keep the team on track and notify the sponsor or champion about progress. In a DMAIC project, milestones are generally set at the end of each phase (Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, and Control). However, teams can set custom milestones, and sponsors might require specific milestones if they're approving large resource or funding requests for a project.

You can also set up milestones within a team setting to manage goals and tasks; these milestones can be kept internal to the team. For example, a team working for a sandwich shop chain hopes to improve the process by which sandwiches are assembled. They set the following milestones:

Define: January 21
Measure: February 12
Analyze: February 22
Improve: March 15
Control: April 10

The milestone dates are when the team or the Black Belt will meet with the sponsor to present each project phase's findings or results. Each date gives the team something to work toward. However, the team determined certain tasks need to happen during the Measure phase. First, they need to build a few term definitions, so everyone's aligned when discussing measurements. Second, the team needs to collect data on the temperature ingredients are stored and cooked at. Finally, the team wants to actively observe sandwich shop employees, to measure how long it takes to make various sandwiches.

The team can set internal milestones for the Measure phase, setting that the definitions will be built by January 25, the temperature data collected by February 5, and the timing data collected by February 10.

By breaking each phase, and each larger task, into smaller pieces, it's easier for the team to stay on track and finish the work. Smaller tasks feel more manageable, so they're more likely to get done.

### Budgets

Teams, and especially team leaders, always need to worry about project budgets. Although success is assessed by end customers in terms of performance, quality, and satisfaction, Six Sigma teams also answer to corporate leadership. For leaders, success is also measured in terms of time and budget. A strong timeline and good milestones help you meet time requirements, and an understanding of financial drivers, strong communication, and financial oversight help you keep a project on budget.

One challenge in dealing with budgets on a Six Sigma project is that not every team member is always fully aware of the financial drivers. In some cases, financial information might even be restricted; employers generally don't want specific data about employee compensation made public to various team members, for example. Some information and analysis might need to be handled exclusively by a Black Belt leading the project in these cases, especially if the data is critical or sensitive.

Outside of sensitive-data concerns, process improvement projects work best when every team member is informed about as many drivers and as much data as possible. When teams know how much funding a champion is willing to pursue on their behalf, they can make realistic decisions about how to improve a process. Sometimes the solution most likely to generate the biggest improvement isn't viable because of budget. If an improvement project has a $50,000 budget, the team can't implement a solution requiring an $80,000 capital investment in machinery, for example.

Budget concerns vary by organization. At some organizations, leaders are more concerned with a team's specific spending, including expenses for new equipment, hiring new staff, or buying new products or software. Some organizations take a more granular approach to project budgets, factoring in the expense of the hours the team spends on the project, as well as the expenses tied to training and implementing a solution outside the team setting.

Six Sigma team leaders need to make sure they understand how leaders and organizations manage project budgets. Working with an organization or sponsor for the first time means having honest, thorough conversations about how budgets are calculated, how willing sponsors are to push for budget increases, and what the Six Sigma leader's expected role is in maintaining budgets.

### Well-Defined Measures of Success

Finally, Six Sigma teams need to build a well-defined measure of success. To better manage a Six Sigma project and team, leaders need to make sure every team member, leader, and sponsor agrees on what success means. If success isn't defined at all, the team risks scope creep and getting lost in a project that never seems to end. If success isn't well defined, teams risk finishing a project without satisfying the customer, the sponsor, or every team member. If a sponsor and the team don't agree on what success looks like, the team might feel it finished a successful project, while leadership believes the project was a failure.

In the end, successfully managing a Six Sigma team depends on many of the same concepts as successful leadership in other endeavors. Choosing the right people, being clear about expectations, approaching the work in an organized way, and being honest and open about progress helps every team member succeed and add value.
